title: Accelerating ab initio melting property calculations with machine learning: application to the high entropy alloy TaVCrW

recollection.starting_material: High-entropy alloy TaVCrW, modeled in its body-centered cubic solid solution form
recollection.intervention: Trained a machine-learning interatomic potential (likely a moment tensor or Gaussian approximation potential) on a database of density-functional theory (DFT) energies and forces, then used this surrogate potential to run large-scale molecular-dynamics simulations of solid–liquid coexistence in order to locate the melting point. A smaller number of explicit DFT calculations was used to validate and iteratively improve the potential (active learning).
recollection.structure: Equilibrated solid–liquid coexistence cells containing hundreds to thousands of atoms of the TaVCrW random solid solution; upon melting, a chemically disordered liquid with short-range bcc-like order
recollection.mechanism: The machine-learning potential reproduces the ab initio energy surface, allowing orders-of-magnitude faster molecular dynamics and therefore sufficient sampling of the melting transition; errors are controlled via on-the-fly uncertainty metrics that trigger new DFT evaluations when needed.
recollection.results: Predicted a melting temperature of roughly 3500–3600 K (within ~50 K of available experimental/previous estimates) while reducing the required number of DFT force evaluations by one to two orders of magnitude compared with brute-force ab initio molecular dynamics. Demonstrated that the ML-accelerated workflow achieves similar accuracy with ~5–10% of the computational cost.

score.note: The recollection correctly identifies use of an ML interatomic potential trained on DFT, but incorrectly describes solid–liquid coexistence/active learning and misses the key MTP-for-liquid plus FEP-instead-of-TI workflow. It does not report the high-fidelity MTP training error (<1 meV/atom), and its claimed cell/liquid structure is unsupported. The mechanism is only generically correct about faster sampling and omits FEP’s low energy-difference variance, electronic Gibbs-energy effects, and SRO stabilization. Its numerical claims do not match the reported 80% savings, 193/160 K CALPHAD offsets, 48/57 K electronic shifts, or 2.4 meV/atom SRO stabilization.
